settings.hogyan_dont_ha_egyszerre: How it decides: if several satellites are above the minimum at once, it follows the one with the highest elevation. It keeps the tracked one until it drops below its minimum, or until another one is higher by at least the switching threshold (and the minimum tracking time has elapsed). This way it does not drop a satellite passing overhead for one that has just appeared.

help.sdr_beallitasa_egyszer_kell:
Setting up SDR++ (once)
  1. SDR++ → Module Manager → add the 'rigctl_server' module.
  2. In the 'Rigctl Server' panel set the port to 4532 (or the same as here), then start it (Start).
  3. The Recorder module must be available – the AOS/LOS commands start and stop it.
  4. If SDR++ runs on another computer: enter that computer's IP address here in Settings, and the SDR++ server must not listen on 127.0.0.1 only.

Usage
  • 'Add satellite': NORAD ID → Search → choose the frequency to follow from the list → Save.
  • The frequency can be changed later ('Edit / frequency'); tracking can be switched on/off per satellite, or the satellite can be deleted. The big button at the top switches the whole tracking on/off.
  • There are three modes (top): 'Follow the selected satellite' – the satellite you select in the list gets its Doppler frequency sent to SDR++ continuously (recording only runs above the minimum elevation); 'Automatic switching' – the elevation rules decide which one is followed; 'Follow only the selected passes' – see the next point.
  • Following a single pass: click a pass in the list, then 'Follow only this pass'. The program then controls SDR++ only during the scheduled pass(es) (above the minimum elevation) and otherwise does not touch it. Several passes can be scheduled; expired ones are removed automatically.
  • Frequency: the big display shows the Doppler-corrected receive frequency (display only). Click the digits of the 'Base frequency' display (top/bottom) or scroll to change the nominal frequency – it is saved at once, and the Doppler keeps being calculated around the new base frequency.
  • The program updates the TLEs at start-up and every 6 hours if they are older than 12 hours.


What do the two tables show?
  • UPPER table ('Tracked satellites'): for each satellite it shows the NEXT suitable pass – the "what comes next" view. The 'Current status' column tells you what is going on NOW (e.g. below the horizon, up but too low, tracked).
  • LOWER table ('Passes in the next 24 hours'): ALL passes of the selected satellite – the "what happens when" view. The ▶ marks the next suitable pass (the same one as in the upper table).
  • A 'suitable' pass: its peak elevation reaches the satellite's minimum + the hysteresis (Settings). A pass that does not is not tracked ("no (max. < 20°)").
  • The "Min. el." column: the satellite's own minimum; "glob." means the general value (Settings). The dashed yellow circle on the sky plot is the minimum of the selected satellite.

What do the colours mean?
  • Green row (upper): the program is tracking this satellite right now. Green row (lower): a trackable pass.
  • Purple row: another suitable satellite is up AT THE SAME TIME (clash). The 'At the same time' column shows which one and its max. elevation: ▲ = the other is higher, ▼ = the other is lower. Click the text of the column to jump to that satellite/pass. The upper table only shows the clash of the NEXT pass, the lower one of every pass.
  • Red row (lower, "✖ skipped manually"): you skipped this pass; the program does not track it.
  • Grey row: a satellite that is switched off, or a pass that is too low.
  • Blue row: the currently selected row. Blue ▶: the next suitable pass.
  • Satellites tab, red row: this satellite is sending AOS/LOS commands to SDR++ right now.

Sky plot (right side)
  • By default the satellites that are up right now are shown, each in its own colour. If you select a pass in the lower table, its path is shown in green (AOS, highest point, LOS, minute marks); the grey part is below the minimum.
  • The paths of clashing satellites, clipped to the common time, are shown in RED, with their name and max. elevation.

Buttons under the lower table
  • 'Follow only this pass (schedule on/off)': schedules the selected pass (blue/green marking, "will be tracked").
  • 'Skip / restore pass': switches tracking off for this one pass only (e.g. in a clash). It is remembered after a restart too.
  • 'Clear all scheduled passes': removes every scheduled pass.
  • 'Hide path': removes the path from the sky plot.
  • 'Original state' (upper): restores the automatic decision – clears manual skips and schedules, and switches every satellite on again (frequencies and thresholds are not touched). If you clicked around and made a mess, start over with this.

Satellites tab
  • All added satellites in one list: name, NORAD, frequency, mode, minimum elevation, AOS/LOS to SDR++, tracking, next pass, max. elevation, when the TLE was downloaded.
  • Click the ✓ column to switch a satellite on/off; click the 'AOS/LOS to SDR++' column to set whether that satellite sends AOS/LOS commands (the general switch in Settings must also be on, otherwise it says "no (global setting off)"). Double-click: edit.
  • The list can be copied to the clipboard or saved as CSV.

TLE (orbit data)
  • 'Update TLE (selected)' updates one satellite, 'Update all TLEs' updates all of them; the result is shown in the Log. The automatic update runs at start-up and every 6 hours if the TLE is older than 12 hours.
  • The age of the TLE is shown in the header of the lower table; if it is old, update it, because the orbit calculation becomes less accurate.

Where is the data saved?
  • In the 'data' folder next to the program (config.json and backups): satellite list, settings, manual skips, schedules. Copy the folder to move the whole setup to another computer.
  • The 'Save list' / 'Load list' buttons (Satellites tab, below the list) save or load only the satellite list (satellites, frequencies and their settings) – your station position is not included, so it is safe to share with others. When loading you can choose: add to the existing ones, or replace the whole list.

Refining your position
  Enter the exact position of the antenna with 6 decimals, e.g. 47.497912 / 19.040235 – this is accurate to about 10 cm. A 6-character locator is only accurate to about 4–5 km, so it is just a fallback. The more exact the position, the more exact the pass times and the Doppler. You can read the exact coordinate on a phone map (long-press the place) or read it from a USB GPS (NMEA).
  It is enough to paste a coordinate copied from Google Maps, like "47.497912, 19.040235", into the Latitude or Longitude field – it fills both fields. Degrees-minutes-seconds (47°29'52.5"N) and a decimal comma also work. The fields tidy themselves into one format when you leave them (6 decimals). Use the 'Show on Google Maps' button to check where the antenna is; the 'Apply and save' button makes it final.
